=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s assessment

**Do not accept this package as settled.** The Seller’s “STANDARD”, “FINAL” and “cleared by both sides” labels are not evidence of Buyer approval. Nor do unsupported market assertions establish that these terms suit this deal. Verify any actual principal-level agreements with Wattlebridge.

The main problem is cumulative: broad disclosures and deemed Buyer knowledge could defeat warranty claims, while a low cap, short deadlines and “all Claims” language could undermine even expressly negotiated protections.

This review is based on the extracts and Disclosure Letter—not the full SPA or underlying DD documents. The disclosed uncertainties should not be treated as proven breaches, but several require resolution before Completion.

## Material issues and pushback

### 1. Liability limitations could swallow the Buyer’s protections
**Clauses 9.3, 12.1–12.3, 12.8, 13 and 20.5**

The AUD 4.8 million general warranty cap is 20% of price. Whether that is acceptable depends on diligence, recovery security and the protections outside it—not the Seller’s assertion of market practice.

The greater concern is applying limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to **all Claims of any nature**. This could restrict specific indemnities, tax claims, repayment obligations, completion adjustments and claims concerning title.

**Push back:**
- Confine the general warranty regime expressly to general warranty claims.
- Set out a clear exceptions and precedence provision covering fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, debt discharge, price adjustments and other payment obligations.
- Carve out Seller fraud and fraudulent concealment, and preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Do not assume that a contractual non-reliance provision validly eliminates all statutory remedies.
- Preserve enforcement of Completion obligations and appropriate equitable relief.

### 2. Title and capacity should not share the general warranty cap and deadline

A defective acquisition of the shares is qualitatively different from an ordinary business warranty breach. Limiting recovery to AUD 4.8 million after paying AUD 24 million leaves the Buyer seriously exposed.

**Push back:** Seek a separate cap of at least the purchase price for fundamental/title/capacity warranties, no de minimis or basket, and a materially longer claim period, settled with NSW counsel by reference to the execution form and applicable limitation rules.

DD-012 is evidence of registered ownership, **not complete verification of transferable, unencumbered title**. Verify the share capital, issue and transfer history, options and other rights, encumbrances and required approvals. Require effective transfer documents and registration of Wattlebridge at Completion.

### 3. Thresholds and time limits reduce practical recovery

The AUD 250,000 basket is deductible: the Buyer bears that amount even once the threshold is crossed. A claim must also **exceed** AUD 25,000, potentially excluding repeated smaller losses.

Eighteen months may not capture latent tax, IP or other problems. Extending this deadline to every Claim is particularly objectionable.

**Push back:**
- Seek a tipping basket and lower thresholds; aggregate claims arising from related facts.
- Exclude fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities from general thresholds.
- Seek a longer general warranty period, with separate periods appropriate to tax and identified risks.
- Ensure timely notified claims survive the deadline; permit reasonable estimates and later supplementation. Check for separate, short litigation commencement deadlines.

### 4. General disclosure and deemed knowledge could hollow out the warranties
**Schedule 7, clause 8.3 and Disclosure Letter §§1.1–1.2**

Disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in a data room, plus public records, is excessively broad. “Discoverable” knowledge goes further still: the Buyer could lose protection for matters it never actually identified. Adviser knowledge creates another expansive attribution route.

**Push back:**
- Require fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter, mapped to the relevant warranty.
- Reject blanket disclosure of public records and documents merely referred to in other documents. Freeze and retain an agreed data-room index and archive.
- Delete constructive/discoverable knowledge and broad adviser attribution. If a knowledge exclusion is unavoidable, restrict it to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel of the relevant facts and breach.
- State that disclosure and knowledge do not qualify specific indemnities, fundamental warranties or express Completion obligations unless specifically agreed.

**Known risks need affirmative contractual protection:** a disclosure may qualify a warranty without funding or fixing the underlying problem.

### 5. Bluefen: a material customer dependency remains unresolved
**Clauses 3 and 6.3; DD-002**

Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue. The letter confirms there is no final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions. Delivering a consent document alone may therefore be insufficient.

**Push back:** Make Completion conditional on effective consent and satisfaction of the applicable clause 11.3 conditions, without adverse contract changes unless Buyer-approved. Require supporting evidence, a long-stop date and Buyer termination rights. Reasonable endeavours should supplement—not replace—the condition. Any waiver should be the Buyer’s decision.

### 6. Riverlark: post-Completion release conflicts with a debt-free acquisition
**Clauses 2 and 7; DD-003**

Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding, with no final discharge. The Buyer should not acquire the company subject to the lender’s security and rely on a later release.

**Push back:** Require a verified payout figure, including interest and fees, and a controlled Completion funds flow that repays the lender directly. Obtain binding release arrangements effective at Completion, with subsequent registry processing tightly controlled. Deal with relevant guarantees and change-control requirements as well.

Ensure the debt is deducted or otherwise funded consistently with the agreed AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free mechanics, **without double counting**.

### 7. Completion bonuses are missing from the funds flow
**DD-005**

The AUD 420,000 bonuses are conditional obligations, not necessarily amounts already payable. Nevertheless, Completion may trigger a real company cash cost. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not allocate that cost contractually.

**Push back:** Expressly allocate the transaction-triggered bonuses and applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs to the Seller. Reflect them in the price adjustment or funded Completion arrangements, with a true-up for uncertainties and no double counting. Verify continued-employment conditions, payment timing and the employing entity.

### 8. Ironquay: paying a fee is not the same as securing usable IP
**Clause 11.1; DD-004 and DD-010**

The records suggest AUD 180,000 is open, but do not independently establish non-payment. More importantly, SOW3 ownership transfer depends on cleared payment of every relevant fee. A payment-only indemnity may not cover defective title, lost use, replacement costs or third-party claims.

**Push back:** Obtain payment reconciliation and confirmation, and an effective confirmatory assignment before or at Completion. Verify the rights required to use and commercialise the materials, including relevant contractor and third-party rights. Broaden the specific indemnity to the identified ownership/use exposure and associated losses, with bespoke limits and duration rather than the general warranty regime.

### 9. Export/privacy incident: unresolved, not demonstrably immaterial
**Clause 4.6 and Schedule 6; DD-006**

There is evidence of a download link sent to an unintended external address, potentially involving around 1,240 records. There is **not yet evidence establishing access, exact scope, a notifiable breach or quantified loss**. The Seller’s reassurance is therefore premature.

**Push back:** Require prompt investigation, evidence preservation, containment and a documented assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations. Obtain updates through Completion and agree responsibility for lawful remediation and notifications.

Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-Completion incident, including reasonable investigation, remediation and third-party claim costs, and regulatory amounts only where lawfully indemnifiable. Consider a retention or Completion condition if investigation reveals material exposure.

### 10. Sandbar renewals: classify before allocating AUD 330,000
**DD-008 and DD-011**

Neither “ordinary-course costs” nor “Seller debt” is established. The three related renewals should be assessed together, including whether commitments have been split across any approval threshold.

**Push back:** Verify execution dates, scope, service periods, termination rights, accruals and approvals. Allocate through debt, working capital, prepayments or a specific adjustment as appropriate. Buyer may properly bear genuine post-Completion operating costs; Seller should bear amounts allocated to it under the agreed economics or arising from covenant breaches. Avoid double counting.

### 11. Tax and broader IP protection remain open

“Settled under the general regime” is not an adequate answer. Tax exposures can emerge well after 18 months, and IP ownership and licensing are central to a SaaS acquisition.

**Push back:** Seek a separate tax covenant/indemnity for relevant pre-Completion liabilities, appropriate tax warranties, longer survival and tailored claims-control provisions. Review IP ownership, licensing, infringement and contractor-chain protections independently of the narrow Ironquay indemnity.

### 12. Lease and Mossvale: do not invent consent requirements
**DD-007 and DD-009**

The lease disclosure identifies notification, not landlord consent. Mossvale’s assignment restriction does not, by itself, establish a consent requirement for a share sale.

**Action:** Check the full contracts for change-control and other relevant provisions. Require any actual notices or consents, but do not make unsupported consent demands.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Protect Completion:** effective Bluefen consent and conditions; Riverlark repayment and security release; verified share title; satisfactory Ironquay rights.
2. **Protect the economics:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs; classify renewals; reconcile all amounts with the debt-free/cash-free price mechanics.
3. **Restore meaningful recourse:** narrow “all Claims” limitations, reject blanket disclosure/deemed knowledge, and separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity protections.
4. **Resolve uncertainty:** complete the incident investigation and obtain updated evidence through Completion.
5. **Secure recovery:** assess Seller creditworthiness and seek an appropriately sized retention, escrow or guarantee where needed.

**Bottom line:** Do not exchange known and unresolved risks for warranties that the disclosure and limitations package may render ineffective. Require evidence, Completion protections, explicit cost allocation and enforceable residual recourse.
